items.hypothesis: Control for today's slide-count test: 6 slides, statement hook ('Your dreams rarely replay your day', 33 characters), payoff on slide 2, split scene, night theme. Baseline watched-full % against 1003-2 (5 slides).
items.caption:
Your dreams rarely replay your day.
In a 2003 study, 29 people kept a daily log and wrote down dreams for 14 days. About 65% of 299 dream reports were judged to reflect recent life, yet whole-episode replays appeared in no more than 1 to 2%. Pieces, not reruns.

Same series, statement hook ('People who dreamed of a maze got better at it', 43 characters), payoff on slide 2, split scene, night theme, caption structure. Expected: higher watched-full % than the control because the end arrives sooner.
items.caption:
People who dreamed of a maze got better at it.
In a 2010 Harvard nap study, 4 of 50 nappers reported dreams or sleep-onset thoughts about a virtual maze and improved about tenfold more than other nappers. A tiny group and a correlation; waking thoughts about the maze did not predict it.

items.caption:
You're taller in the morning.
In a 1984 study of 8 men, height peaked at about 7:30 on waking and was about 2 cm (1.1 %) lower by midnight. The discs between the spine bones lose volume after a day upright and regain it when you lie down: lab studies simulated a night with about 6 hours of lying down. The amount varies by person.

items.caption: Why do dreams vanish by breakfast? Your brain enters REM sleep several times a night, but the sleeping brain is bad at saving new memories. In one study, frequent dream recallers spent about twice as long briefly awake at night. What's the last dream you remember?

items.caption:
Dreaming of being chased?
In a survey of 1,181 students, being chased was the most common of 55 dream themes: over 80% had dreamed it at least once. One idea is threat rehearsal, still debated.
Chased, falling, or late for an exam: which one comes back for you?
